statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether drinking at a young age causes alcohol problems in adulthood, or whether the same family, genetic and personal factors lead to both. In general-population cohorts that recorded the age of the first drink during adolescence, an earlier first drink went with more adult drinking or alcohol problems in some analyses and not in others, and the association often shrank when other risk factors were taken into account. A systematic review found only four such cohorts up to January 2013 (two in the USA and two in Norway; 447 to 1,311 people each; five reports; no meta-analysis; confidence in the review rated critically low on its study card): in an Oslo school cohort, a later first drink went with less drinking and fewer problems at 18 to 21, with control only for parents' and peers' influence; in a US community cohort, a first drink before 11 went with problem drinking by 31 (odds ratios 2.39 and 5.75, depending on where the first drink happened, against a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering) but not after adjustment for further risk factors, while feeling drunk at the first drink remained a predictor; in the Young in Norway cohort, drinking by 13 to 14, compared with a later first drink, went with frequent intoxication (odds ratio 1.5, 95% CI 1.2 to 1.9) and with an AUDIT score of 8 or more, a screen for risky drinking (1.6, 1.3 to 2.1), at 26 to 27, adjusted for gender, both falling to 1.2 (0.9 to 1.6) when conduct problems in adolescence were also taken into account; in a Seattle cohort of people who started drinking before 21, the age of the first drink was not associated with adult alcohol misuse or with alcohol dependence at any follow-up, but, compared with a first drink at 11 to 14, a first drink before 11 went with a past-year dependence diagnosis at more of the interviews held every 3 years from 21 to 33 (odds ratio 1.68) and, in a later report, with more chronic dependence, essentially unchanged across four adjusted models. The review's abstract says that rigorous adjustment markedly weakens or removes such associations, which its own Seattle summary contradicts; the authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting earlier leads to adult problems, and found that feeling drunk at the first drink and the start of regular drinking went with adult problems more strongly than the age of the first drink (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). In a Minnesota cohort of twins born 1977 to 1984 (1,512 twins at about age 11; drinking reported at the assessment planned for age 14, held at a mean age of 14.8; outcomes at about 25), twins who had drunk without their parents' permission by that assessment already differed beforehand from twins who had not, notably in delinquent behaviour and in their parents' drinking and smoking; after weighting for 29 characteristics of the twins and their families measured at about 11, early drinking was associated with a higher adult alcohol-use score (standardized coefficient 0.57, SE 0.06), and within twin pairs who differed in early drinking the association was a little over a third as large but remained (0.21, SE 0.09, in all pairs; 0.22, SE 0.10, in identical pairs, who share all their genes and their family; the estimates for identical and fraternal pairs did not differ significantly), whereas within identical pairs early drinking was not clearly associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.17, SE 0.14) (Irons et al., 2015). Twin comparisons remove what co-twins share, not differences between them such as their own early use of tobacco or other drugs. Grant & Dawson (1998), the national survey analysis of age at first drug use and drug use disorders, is not yet read. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does drinking young lead to alcohol problems later? This is not known. In the few studies that followed young people over time, in the US and Norway, drinking early went with more drinking problems as an adult in some studies, but in others the link went away once other risks, such as behaviour problems in adolescence, were taken into account. Feeling drunk at the first drink and starting to drink regularly went with later problems more strongly than the age of the first drink. In US twins, the twin who had drunk without their parents' permission by about age 15 drank more as an adult than the twin who had not, even in identical twins, though the difference was smaller than when all the young people in the study were compared; in identical twins, early drinking was not clearly linked to later symptoms of an alcohol disorder. Twin studies cannot rule out other differences between twins, such as smoking or other drug use. See the contested question.
population: Young people in general-population cohorts followed from adolescence into adulthood: four cohorts in the USA and Norway in a systematic review (447 to 1,311 people each) and Minnesota twins born 1977–1984 (1,512 at about age 11)
exposure: An earlier first drink (more than a few sips; definitions differed, from before 11 to by 13–14), recorded in adolescence; in the twin study, drinking without parental permission, or being intoxicated, by the assessment planned for age 14 (mean age 14.8)
comparator: People who started drinking later (in the Rutgers cohort, a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering; in the Seattle cohort, a first drink at 11 to 14); in the twin study, twins who had not, including their own co-twin
outcome: Adult drinking, alcohol problems and alcohol dependence (consumption indices, problem scales, AUDIT, DSM-IV symptom counts or diagnoses, at 18 to about 33)
magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Maimaris & McCambridge (2014), four cohorts, no pooling: Oslo (n = 522) structural coefficients −3.465 for debut age on consumption and −13.828 on a problem index (p < 0.0001), with parental and peer control only; Rutgers (n = 447, people with data at every wave) first drink before 11, OR 2.39 (95% CI 1.10–5.20) at a family gathering and 5.75 (1.53–21.54) elsewhere, both against a first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering, for lifetime problem drinking by 31, not significant in the fully adjusted model (coefficient −0.0631), feeling drunk at the first drink 0.3848 (p < 0.0001); Seattle (n = 808 who started drinking before 21), against a first drink at 11–14, for a first drink before 11, at 15–17 and at 18–20: misuse at any follow-up ORs 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64, dependence at any follow-up 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35 (all p > 0.05); first drink before 11 and the number of interviews (every 3 years from 21 to 33) with a past-year dependence diagnosis OR 1.68 (p < 0.05; no intervals), later report (n = 706) chronicity β 0.44 unadjusted and 0.45 to 0.53 in four adjusted models; Young in Norway (n = 1,311), drinking by 13–14 against later, adjusted for gender: frequent intoxication OR 1.5 (1.2–1.9) and AUDIT 8 or more 1.6 (1.3–2.1); both 1.2 (0.9–1.6) with conduct problems added. Irons et al. (2015), drinking without parental permission by the age-14 assessment (mean age 14.8), standardized β (SE): adult alcohol-use index, weighted 0.57 (0.06), within all discordant pairs 0.21 (0.09), identical pairs 0.22 (0.10), fraternal pairs 0.20 (0.14) (within-pair estimates 0.37 and 0.39 of the weighted one, editors' calculation; zygosity did not significantly moderate any within-pair effect); alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms, weighted 0.36, all pairs 0.24 (0.11), identical 0.17 (0.14), fraternal 0.34 (0.16); intoxication by the age-14 assessment and alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms within all pairs 0.29 (0.15). The twin study's printed p-values are not used (card reporting issue).

risk_of_bias.note: The cohorts adjusted for different, incomplete sets of confounders (only one for family history; none for genetic liability), some possibly on the causal path; confidence in the review is critically low (card sc_maimaris_2014: AMSTAR 2, no protocol, no list of excluded studies, single-reviewer screening); in the twin study, confounders not shared by co-twins, such as their own early tobacco or drug use, were not measured, and 12% were not seen at about 25 (card sc_irons_2015: ROBINS-E, some concerns).

inconsistency.note: The association survived adjustment in some analyses (Seattle chronicity; within twin pairs for adult drinking) and not in others (Rutgers, Young in Norway, Seattle misuse and any dependence; identical pairs for abuse or dependence symptoms).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: four cohorts in the USA and Norway and one Minnesota twin cohort, with outcomes from drinking scores to symptom counts and chronic dependence, all stated.

imprecision.note: Cohorts of 447 to 1,311 people with small exposure groups (a first drink before 11); no intervals for the Seattle estimates; the identical-pair estimates rest on roughly 97 discordant pairs (editors' estimate on the study card), with standard errors close to the estimates.

publication_bias.note: The review judges publication bias a profound threat but could not test it; not rated down separately, since the certainty is already at its floor.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision: very low, the floor. Counted once: the two Seattle reports share one cohort (four cohorts, not five studies). The twin study's printed p-values are not valid (card reporting issue), so significance is judged from coefficients and standard errors. The claim concerns cause, so its relation is insufficient evidence; the association of an earlier first drink with more adult drinking in several cohorts is reported in it, not rated as a separate claim. Grant & Dawson (1998), on age at first drug use, is not yet read; the alcohol landmark from the same survey (Grant & Dawson, 1997) has no reference record in the library. Status contested: credible analyses point both ways and the review's own authors say the answer is not known, so the six-part debate box applies.

debate.question: Does drinking at a young age cause alcohol problems in adulthood, or do the same family, genetic and personal factors lead both to early drinking and to later problems?
debate.evidence_yes: In the Seattle cohort, a first drink before 11 went with more chronic alcohol dependence to age 33, and the association was essentially unchanged after adding peer, school, behavioural and substance-use factors in four models (β 0.44 unadjusted, 0.45 to 0.53 adjusted), with none of the three alternative explanations tested supported; in the Oslo cohort, a later first drink went with less drinking and fewer problems at 18 to 21 (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). In Minnesota twins, drinking without parental permission by the assessment planned for age 14 (mean age 14.8), recorded at that assessment, was associated with a higher adult alcohol-use score after weighting for 29 childhood characteristics (0.57) and within twin pairs who differed in early drinking (0.21), including identical pairs, who share all their genes and their family (0.22, SE 0.10); across all discordant pairs it was also associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.24, SE 0.11). The authors read the within-pair results as supporting an effect of early drinking, while noting that confounders not shared by co-twins could explain them (Irons et al., 2015).
debate.evidence_no: In two of the four general-population cohorts the association did not survive adjustment: in the Rutgers cohort a first drink before 11 went with problem drinking by 31 (odds ratios 2.39 and 5.75, against a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering) only before adjustment for further risk factors, and in the Young in Norway cohort drinking by 13 to 14 went with frequent intoxication and risky drinking at 26 to 27 (1.5 and 1.6, adjusted for gender) only until adolescent conduct problems were taken into account (both 1.2, 0.9 to 1.6); in the Seattle cohort the age of the first drink was not associated with adult alcohol misuse or with dependence at any follow-up; the Oslo estimate controlled only for parents' and peers' influence; feeling drunk at the first drink and starting regular drinking went with adult problems more strongly than the age of the first drink; and the review's authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting earlier leads to adult problems (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). In the twin study, twins who drank by the assessment planned for age 14 already differed beforehand in delinquent behaviour and in their parents' drinking and smoking; for the adult alcohol-use score the within-pair association was a little over a third of the weighted one (0.21 against 0.57, ratio 0.37; editors' calculation); and within identical pairs early drinking was not clearly associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.17, SE 0.14), nor was intoxication by that assessment across all pairs (0.29, SE 0.15) (Irons et al., 2015).
debate.neither_can_show: No randomized evidence exists, since the age of a first drink cannot be assigned at random. The cohorts recorded the first drink in adolescence, which avoids recalling it decades later, but they can adjust only for what they measured: only one adjusted for family history of alcohol problems, none controlled for genetic liability, and adjusting for peers or behaviour that early drinking may itself change can remove part of a real effect. In two of the four cohorts the first drink of late starters was not recorded in adolescence or 3 years before the outcome. Co-twin comparisons remove everything twins share (all genes in identical pairs, half in fraternal pairs, and the family they grew up in) but not what differs between them, such as their own early smoking, other drug use or friends, and random error in reporting early drinking shrinks within-pair estimates on its own; the identical-pair estimates rest on roughly 97 discordant pairs, so a non-significant result there is not evidence of no effect. Both twin exposures were yes-or-no, so nothing is known about how much the young people drank.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). An earlier first drink goes with more adult drinking in several cohorts, and part of that link reflects differences that were there before the first drink, such as behaviour problems and family drinking: in two of four cohorts the link disappeared after adjustment, and in twins it was a little over a third as large within pairs as in the comparison weighted for childhood characteristics. Within identical twins, early drinking still went with more adult drinking, which leaves room for an effect of early drinking itself, but it was not clearly linked to symptoms of alcohol use disorder, and the twin design cannot exclude differences between co-twins. The evidence read here cannot say whether delaying the first drink would reduce adult alcohol problems; in the review, feeling drunk at the first drink and early regular drinking were more strongly linked to adult problems than the age of the first drink.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Pooled analyses of identical twin pairs who differ in early drinking across several twin registries, large enough to estimate effects on alcohol use disorder precisely, with early drinking recorded repeatedly (age, amount, intoxication) and the twins' own earlier behaviour and substance use measured; harmonized analyses of several large birth or school cohorts with the first drink recorded as it happens and the same confounders; and natural experiments that shift the age of first drinking for reasons unrelated to the person, such as changes in minimum legal drinking ages.
